description: This section of Logical Reasoning evaluates the strength of arguments regarding a specific decision or issue. The primary objective is to logically determine which argument is strong and which is weak.

sections.title: Basic Concept
sections.description: In Statement and Argument questions, a statement is provided followed by two or more arguments. The candidate must evaluate the arguments strictly in the context of the given statement.

key_concepts.explanation: An argument that is directly related to the statement and is practically, factually, and logically true. It is usually based on established facts, universal truths, and public interest.
An argument that is superficial, ambiguous, or irrelevant to the core statement. It often involves incomplete information, personal opinions, or extreme assumptions.

sections.title: Identification of Strong Arguments
sections.description: For an argument to be classified as strong, it must fulfill specific logical conditions and remain highly relevant to the premise.

results: The argument should be grounded in science, constitutional law, or established facts.
It should promote the broader interest of the public, society, country, or environment.
If the advice or remedy suggested in the argument is practically capable of solving the core problem mentioned in the statement, it is considered a strong argument.

sections.title: Identification of Weak Arguments
sections.description: Certain types of arguments are universally considered weak because they lack a solid logical foundation.

key_concepts.explanation: If the argument uses absolute or extreme words like 'only', 'always', or 'definitely' without solid backing, it is usually a weak argument.

results: When the argument suggests imitating another country, state, or individual (e.g., 'Yes, because it is done in America too').
Arguments based solely on comparison are always considered weak.
Arguments that lack a clear, definitive reason and are based merely on someone's unverified assumption or personal bias.

sections.title: Steps to Solve Questions
sections.description: Following a systematic analytical process is necessary to accurately select the correct argument without personal bias.

steps.title: Unbiased Analysis of Statement
steps.detail: Read the statement carefully and assume the information provided is absolutely true. Do not introduce your personal opinions or external assumptions.

steps.title: Initial Evaluation of Arguments
steps.detail: Read each argument independently. Check if it provides a valid and logical reason to support its 'Yes' or 'No' stance.

steps.title: Check Relevance
steps.detail: Ensure the argument directly addresses the context of the statement and does not deviate into unrelated topics.

steps.title: Final Decision
steps.detail: Categorize the argument strictly as strong or weak based on the rules, and select the corresponding correct option.

sections.title: Standard Answer Options
sections.description: Competitive exams generally provide standard multiple-choice options to conclude the evaluation of the arguments.

cases.condition: Only Argument I or II is Strong
results: Option A: Only argument I is strong (selected when only the first argument provides a solid, logical reason).
Option B: Only argument II is strong (selected when only the second argument provides a solid, logical reason).
Option C: Either argument I or II is strong (selected when both arguments contradict each other but are logically strong in their own separate contexts).
Option D: Neither argument I nor II is strong (selected when both arguments fail the test of logic and relevance).
Option E: Both argument I and II are strong (selected when both arguments present independent, valid, and logical reasons addressing the statement).
